feedback: If a learner places a fraction on the wrong side of 1/2, return to comparing the numerator with half the denominator.
If a learner is unsure whether a fraction is near 0 or near 1, check how close the numerator is to 0 or to the denominator (e.g. 1/5 is near 0, 4/5 is near 1).
If a learner struggles to compare across the two denominators, align the two labelled sequences and read off which mark lies further right.
activities.intendedInsight: A number line anchored to 0, 1/2 and 1 gives fractions a magnitude and a 'side of 1/2' (and a sense of nearness to 0 or 1), so many comparisons can be read off directly; dual labelling lets two different denominators be compared on one line.
learnerActions: Use a number line marked only 0, 1/2, 1 and place common fractions where they belong relative to those landmarks; for each, say whether it is more than, equal to, or less than one half.
Decide whether 4/9 is more or less than a half by comparing 4 with half of 9 (4.5): 4 is less than 4.5, so 4/9 < 1/2 — no common denominator needed.
Order 1/5, 4/5, 5/9 using only benchmarks: 1/5 sits just above 0, 5/9 is just over 1/2 (5 is more than 4.5), and 4/5 is near 1, giving 1/5 < 5/9 < 4/5.
For two different denominators, use a dual-labelled line (one unit sequence of marks above the line, the other below) to see where each fraction falls and which is larger.
Explain how the landmarks 0, 1/2 and 1 let you decide a comparison without finding a common denominator.
activities.title: Dual-labelled and benchmark number lines

feedback: If a learner orders by single digits ('7/10 is smallest because 10 is biggest'), rename all three to a common denominator or place them on a 0/½/1 line and compare magnitudes.
If a learner grinds a full common-denominator computation for 5/8 vs 3/7, prompt the quicker 1/2 benchmark.
Reward correct answers that also carry a model-based justification.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent comparison means ordering correctly, choosing an efficient strategy, and justifying with a model — not just getting a final symbol right. Any valid common denominator yields the same order.
learnerActions: Order a set such as 2/3, 3/5, 7/10 from smallest to largest and show working (e.g. common denominator 30: 3/5 = 18/30, 2/3 = 20/30, 7/10 = 21/30, giving 3/5 < 2/3 < 7/10).
Answer a quick benchmark question: 'Is 5/8 more or less than 1/2?' and justify.
Rename both fractions of a pair to a shared common denominator before comparing, and check the order you get.
Sort a set of fractions into 'less than 1/2' and 'more than 1/2'.
Keep the same-numerator shortcut in play: with equal numerators, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction (2/3 > 2/5).
Check that a different common denominator does not change the order (e.g. using 60 instead of 30 gives the same ordering).
activities.title: Check and consolidate ordering and benchmark decisions
